title: Comment on FR Doc # 2020-00261
comment_text:
On behalf of Amnesty International and our more than seven million members and supporters worldwide, we hereby submit this statement in response to the request for information on the "Draft Memorandum to the Heads of Executive Departments and Agencies, Guidance for Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Application" (henceforth "AI Memorandum"). Amnesty International ("Amnesty") is an international human rights organization with national Sections in more than 70 countries, including the United States (U.S.)
AMNESTY'S ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ("AI") AND HUMAN RIGHTS INITIATIVE
Amnesty's Artificial Intelligence ("AI") and Human Rights Initiative tackles human rights challenges posed by AI technologies. A core part of the initiative is the enforcement of human rights law to ensure that the development and use of AI does not undermine human rights standards, and instead strengthens such standards where possible.

OVERVIEW
1.AI has the potential to bring positive change for human rights. As noted in the Guidance for Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Applications, the deployment of AI technology "holds the promise to improve safety, fairness, welfare, transparency and other social goals." However, Amnesty believes there are key issues with AI systems that urgently need to be addressed to respect human rights.
2.Global innovation and development of AI technology is being substantially driven by major U.S.-based companies in Silicon Valley. The U.S. is one of a handful of countries that has experienced significant economic gain linked to the development of AI. The U.S. Government therefore has a critical role to play in adopting robust regulatory measures and accountability mechanisms to ensure that AI advances rather than undermines human rights. For the purpose of this paper, Amnesty adopts the definition of artificial intelligence as codified in Section 238(g) of the John S. McCain National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2019, Pub. L. No. 115-232, 132 Stat. 1636, 1695 (August 13, 2018), and also understands that the scope of the potential regulation covered by these regulations applies to "narrow" AI.
3.Amnesty's chief concerns with current AI systems are that:
AI technology is predicted to fuel significant changes to employment in the U.S., particularly through automation of jobs, which will require governmental action to protect U.S. workers' rights.
AI systems collecting and processing vast amounts of personal data create new threats to human rights, notably to the right to privacy on both an individual and societal level.
A growing body of research demonstrates that AI systems are already contributing to discrimination - for example, in policing and criminal justice systems in the U.S. The Toronto Declaration underscores the risks to the right to equality and non- discrimination that are inherent to machine learning, and outlines means of protecting and promoting this right.
The impact of AI on policing and conflict could have extremely dangerous and irreversible implications on international human rights and humanitarian law.
A lack of transparency and accountability in current systems denies those harmed by AI-informed decisions adequate visibility of harms and access to effective remedy.
Innovation in AI technology is being led by powerful corporate actors and has rapidly advanced before appropriate state-based regulatory safeguards have been put in place.

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2020-00261
comment_text:
Request for Comments on a Draft Memorandum to the Heads of Executive Departments and Agencies, "Guidance for Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Applications," (Federal Register Doc. 2020-00261)

Dear Mr. Ray:

The U.S. Council for International Business (USCIB) is pleased to participate in this call for public comments concerning the Office of Management and Budget's draft "Guidance for Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Applications." USCIB is a U.S.-based business association composed of U.S. multinational companies, law firms, and trade associations from every sector of the economy. Importantly, our membership includes a cross-section of leading global companies in the information and communications technology (ICT) sector as well as a diverse array of leader users of ICT technologies and emerging innovations, such as Artificial Intelligence (AI). We appreciate the opportunity to offer both a cross-sectoral and tech-informed perspective on proposed policies or regulations related to AI applications.

As the sole U.S. affiliate of Business at OECD, USCIB members played leading roles shaping the OECD's landmark AI Principles and subsequent OECD Council Recommendation on Artificial Intelligence. USCIB member experts from leading AI innovators such as IBM, Microsoft, Google, and Facebook were tapped to advise development of these principles, which the G20 Trade and Digital Economy Ministers subsequently endorsed at the June 8-9, 2019 meeting in Tsukuba, Japan. Although OMB's proposed AI regulatory guidance is outlined a bit differently from the OECD principles, USCIB members note with favor the high degree to which the OMB proposal aligns substantively with the OECD principles. This constitutes a solid foundation to build upon in considering appropriate policies and regulations for ever-evolving technology.

Key Alignments between OMB Proposed Guidance and OECD AI Principles

We would like to highlight elements of the OMB proposed guidance that are closely aligned with what we developed in the OECD and would like to see implemented in the United States.

Discouraging Premature Regulation - USCIB agrees that pre-emptive regulation risks hampering innovation that ultimately could contribute to economic development, commercial and employment opportunities, and societal well-being. We feel there is great potential for the application of AI in healthcare, "smart city" applications, optimizing and securing telecommunications networks, fraud prevention, financial services, transportation, agriculture, and enabling disabled individuals to become active participants in the digital economy, to name a few. We further concur that a "light touch" approach to regulation of AI is preferable until we develop a clear understanding through further research of how it may be applied beneficially to a variety of use cases, while at the same time addressing privacy, security, and other challenges.

Flexibility - We note that OECD AI Principle 2.3 urges development of a policy environment for AI that supports an "agile transition" from R&D to deployment. OMB's call for performance-based flexible frameworks when developing regulatory and non-regulatory approaches that can adapt to rapid changes and updates to AI applications is in the same spirit.

Safety and Security - USCIB commends OMB for highlighting the need for public trust in AI by designating this as the first principle. We share OMB's view concerning the importance of safety and security issues throughout the AI design, development and operation lifecycle.

Risk Assessment - USCIB strongly agrees that policy and regulatory approaches to AI should be based on consistent application of risk assessment and risk management practices. This concept is the cornerstone of the OECD's 2015 Digital Security Risk Management for Economic and Social Prosperity, which USCIB members also actively shaped as Expert Group participants.

Public Participation - OMB's proposed principles underscore the importance of the public comment process throughout the rulemaking process. They also urge agencies to inform the public and promote awareness of AI standards through the creation of informative documents. This is consistent with OECD's emphasis on initiating public dialogue to enhance understanding of AI and to debate AI-related opportunities and challenges for the economy, society, and the workplace to inform policymakers.

Please see the attached PDF for our comprehensive comments.

Sincerely yours,


Barbara P. Wanner
Vice President, ICT Policy

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2021-16176
comment_text:
NIST is requesting information related to the following topics:
1. The greatest challenges in improving how AI actors manage AI-related risks—where “manage” means identify, assess, prioritize, respond to, or communicate those risks;
*Voluntary Participation and Reporting is likely insufficient. Mandatory reporting must be required.

2. How organizations currently define and manage characteristics of AI trustworthiness and whether there are important characteristics which should be considered in the Framework besides: Accuracy, explainability and interpretability, reliability, privacy, robustness, safety, security (resilience), and mitigation of harmful bias, or harmful outcomes from misuse of the AI;
*A Complete Standard for Hazard Identification and Mitigation, Threat Identification and Risk, and Specific Scoped Vulnerability must be created and maintained for all eternity.

3. How organizations currently define and manage principles of AI trustworthiness and whether there are important principles which should be considered in the Framework besides: Transparency, fairness, and accountability;
*Project Motivation and Specific, Issue-Based, Moral Value Statements with Proof-of-No-Conflict documents must be recorded.

4. The extent to which AI risks are incorporated into different organizations' overarching enterprise risk management—including, but not limited to, the management of risks related to cybersecurity, privacy, and safety;
*At last, Enterprise must formally be welcomed into the fold of Managed Risk, just as Infrastructure and others have before it. There are classifications, Tiers, and Strategies.

5. Standards, frameworks, models, methodologies, tools, guidelines and best practices, and principles to identify, assess, prioritize, mitigate, or communicate AI risk and whether any currently meet the minimum attributes described above;
*Start with the basic inclusions of RAMCAP, and work your way out.

6. How current regulatory or regulatory reporting requirements (e.g., local, state, national, international) relate to the use of AI standards, frameworks, models, methodologies, tools, guidelines and best practices, and principles;
*I envision something like the current practices of Building Planning, with the ongoing practices of Emissions Monitoring, with similar penalties and practices.

7. AI risk management standards, frameworks, models, methodologies, tools, guidelines and best practices, principles, and practices which NIST should consider to ensure that the AI RMF aligns with and supports other efforts;
*Existing Hazard, Threat, Risk, Vulnerability and Resource-Use Planning methods should be used and expanded upon.

8. How organizations take into account benefits and issues related to inclusiveness in AI design, development, use and evaluation—and how AI design and development may be carried out in a way that reduces or manages the risk of potential negative impact on individuals, groups, and society.
*Once again, Mandatory reporting of project Motivations into the public record, with customer/stakeholder accountability from the project owners, is the best and only perceived way.

9. The appropriateness of the attributes NIST has developed for the AI Risk Management Framework. (See above, “AI RMF Development and Attributes”);
10. Effective ways to structure the Framework to achieve the desired goals, including, but not limited to, integrating AI risk management processes with organizational processes for developing products and services for better outcomes in terms of trustworthiness and management of AI risks. Respondents are asked to identify any current models which would be effective. These could include—but are not limited to—the NIST Cybersecurity Framework or Privacy Framework, which focus on outcomes, functions, categories and subcategories and also offer options for developing profiles reflecting current and desired approaches as well as tiers to describe degree of framework implementation; and
*Understanding the existence of AI Agents/Entities as primarily a “Risk to be Reduced with Untold Benefits” drives the contriving of a Risk-Mitigation-First Framework. (please see my attached comments)

11. How the Framework could be developed to advance the recruitment, hiring, development, and retention of a knowledgeable and skilled workforce necessary to perform AI-related functions within organizations.
*(please see my attached comments)

12. The extent to which the Framework should include governance issues, including but not limited to make up of design and development teams, monitoring and evaluation, and grievance and redress.”
*(please see my attached comments)

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2021-16176
comment_text:
The AI Village* welcomes the NIST RFI on Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework. Such a framework is long overdue to confidently adopt AI in production systems, including mission-, security- and safety-critical applications.
Our response is articulated on five axes: (i) concrete and current risk, (ii) actionability, (iii) organizations focus, (iv) case specific and (v) existing and upcoming standards.

More specifically each of those five axes tries to answer a specific need of the framework:

Concrete and current risk: This addresses the lack of adequate and easily manipulable risk definition in the case of AI systems and the current divide between risks faced today in production by organizations and the hypothetical and future risks considered in a number of Reliable AI academic publications. As a strongly industry focused organization, we believe the former should be given immediate priority and the latter should be used primarily as a support vector for threat anticipation.

Actionability: This axis addresses the current difficulty in making AI risk assessments and mitigation operational including both the methodological and tooling gaps in conducting end-to-end AI risk assessments. We identify gaps in enforceability as well as current risk and testing methodologies that will need to be filled ahead of proper AI risk assessment engagements.

Organizational focus: By this axis we address the incentives, budget obtention, team reorganizations, business integration and related organizational challenges that implementers will eventually face in their respective organizations. The framework will need to provide answers on those points to ease its deployment in complex governance schemes.

Case specific: By this axis we seek to address specific challenges that will arise on a case by case basis and which a generic framework might be incapable of covering. In our response, we take specific attention in addressing both large and small organizations, specific industries like finance, ICS and pharmaceuticals etc.

Existing and upcoming standards: Our submission draws heavily from a number of existing and upcoming security, privacy and AI regulations that are listed in appendix A. We curated this list based on their relevance and implementation likelihood in target organizations. The upcoming AI Risk framework should tightly integrate with those to limit conflicts and necessary additional work, thereby facilitating adoption.

Our full response is included in separate file.

*The AI Village is a community of hackers and data scientists working to educate the world on the use and abuse of artificial intelligence in security and privacy. We are academics, IT specialists, security experts, students, philosophers, and concerned citizens.

The following information is contained in the 2021 Technology In Industry Report, compiled and published by Automation Alley in Troy, MI. It is distributed to the members of Automation Alley for their education and benefit.
Foreword
After years of stagnation, punctuated by a global health crisis, the manufacturing sector is poised for a boom—and Industry 4.0 technologies are leading the way.

While the COVID-19 pandemic exposed manufacturing supply chain vulnerabilities, it also demonstrated the power of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, as digital technologies played a critical role in the pandemic response for many companies. It was also a wake-up call to the world that resiliency and agility must have an equal seat at the table to efficiency. These realizations are now placing new pressures on manufacturers to innovate.

Emerging tech continues to transform the world of production—creating competitive advantage for companies and unlocking new value for industry, society and our environment. However, it is also creating profound uncertainty for small and medium-sized manufacturers (SMEs), as well as the global workforce.

Automation Alley, the Industry 4.0 knowledge center, exists to help companies of all sizes navigate the digital transformation. Our annual Technology in Industry Report, a collaboration between regional academic and industry leaders, provides a deep dive into smart technology trends, case studies that demonstrate technology adoption and ROI and action items designed to guide businesses to strategic success.

What we have learned from our collective 2021 research, and through conversations with SMEs, is that their roadblocks to Industry 4.0 adoption are extraordinarily similar. Companies consistently report 1) a lack of technology knowledge and expertise, 2) a lack of financial resources, 3) a lack of awareness of the need and/or relationship to the bottom line, and 4) a lack of visionary leadership and/or cultural appetite for adoption.

Though these roadblocks exist, and they present real challenges for SMEs, we have seen remarkable progress and change over the last several years when it comes to Industry 4.0 awareness and adoption. Here in Michigan, SMEs are much more aware today of Industry 4.0 and the benefits of digital transformation. In addition, SMEs are no longer intimidated by technology, and are becoming much more comfortable with technologies like 3D printing, collaborative robotics and artificial intelligence (to name a few); and more importantly, experimenting with ways these technologies can work together.

The journey ahead will not be smooth sailing, as we adjust to continued pandemic challenges. And as Industry 4.0 accelerates, what you know may or may not be valid going forward. Technology will change the business model in which you’ve always operated.

Success will be measured by how companies large and small commit to building a culture where people feel free to create change; where technology isn’t something we fear, but something we embrace. We applaud the early adopters. Will you be a fast follower?

title: Comment on FR Doc # 211116-0234
comment_text:
This comment has to do with technologies related to artificial intelligence (AI), specifically how HHS – ASPR plans to support development of the RITCA application for use by response partners in emergency medicine and how NIST should partner with DOJ – NIJ to support development of a comparable application for use by law enforcement officers to significantly improve their recovery of latent evidence from crime scenes during their conduct of the preliminary investigations (see provided discussion of the CLEARS proposal).

The ability of law enforcement to solve serious crimes, especially violent crimes, can be enhanced through development of a new technology application that would support their improved effectiveness in the identification and proper collection of physical evidence during their conduct of preliminary investigations. Trends today include field police officers’ access to smart phones and broadband. In support of this recommended action, also consider the greatly accelerated trends in the fields of video conferencing, telehealth/telemedicine, and distance learning. These five trends have provided NIST and DOJ with an opportunity to address a long-standing gap in police effectiveness, which results from a standard resource management practice that typically requires field police officers to first find any “latent” physical evidence at a crime scene, without their having the necessary tools and/or training required, before these officers are expected/allowed to request support from a crime scene investigation specialist. The word “latent” means not visible to the unaided eye, such as minute quantities of bodily fluids for extracting DNA, especially, but also other types of latent physical evidence. As items of latent evidence, such as samples containing DNA, have dramatically increased in importance for both solving and prosecuting serious crimes, there has not yet been any significant changes in police practices that support increased recoveries of these evidence samples during their preliminary investigations. Once a crime scene has been released without an item of evidence having been recovered, then it is very unlikely that there would be any future recovery.

Through the development of an application for smart phones, “teleforensics” could now become a reality for field police officers. NIST and DOJ should partner with HHS – ASPR, who on Nov. 23, 2021, announced their intent to issue a sole source contract to John Hopkins University’s Applied Physics Laboratory to pilot a regional disaster response application for medical responders across jurisdictions (https://sam.gov/opp/c4e73e0842dd40a7b1dcc931f43dfb80/view). “The online- and mobile-based Resource Information Tracking and Medical Communications Application (RITCA) will enable both synchronous and asynchronous peer-to-peer communication between clinicians and local response personnel who can chat and videoconference”, and EMS responders will have moment-of-need access to Just-In-Time Training resources. This RITCA application will also support both data collection for future analytic analysis and real time situational awareness for response partners.

Just as ASPR has identified this proactive path to leverage technology and cultural shifts to address the knowledge gap that exists for EMS responders regarding identification of best procedures in the field to support EMS’ response to complex medical challenges, NIST and DOJ could use these same positive trends to address the knowledge and capabilities gaps that have long existed among field police officers with regard to the requirements for effective identification and proper recovery of ALL available physical evidence during the conduct of the preliminary investigations of serious crimes.

comment_text:
FASTER (Federal Authority for Science, Technology, Entrepreneurship and Research) Federal Labs Act:

See attached file(s)
The federal lab system is an enormous, $50 billion-plus enterprise of internal research and development
(R&D) across the United States. As governments around the world, including China, pour billions of dollars
into advanced technologies, it is imperative that we use our nation’s federal lab ecosystem as effectively
as possible.
However, because federal labs have varying legal authorities, missions, and cultures, their records of local
economic engagement and technology commercialization vary considerably. Universities, by contrast,
have demonstrated a strong record of supporting regional innovation ecosystems through use of place
(creating incubators, research parks, and adjacent innovation districts), talent (allowing university
researchers to be involved with private-sector technology under approved and managed relationships),
and innovation (using intermediary university foundations to take on business aspects of technology
commercialization).
The Federal Authority for Science, Technology, Entrepreneurship, and Research (FASTER) Federal Labs Act
will make it possible for all federal labs to use the tried-and-true tools that universities use for economic
engagement and technology commercialization. The FASTER Federal Labs Act will do this by: (i) allowing
surplus federal land to be used for public-private partnership facilities, (ii) creating clearer pathways for
federal researchers to work with startup companies, and (iii) authorizing a federally charted tech-transfer
organization based on models established at leading research universities. The FASTER Federal Labs Act
will not require significant outlay of federal appropriations as many of its provisions simply give federal
labs greater discretion over deployment of existing resources. The Act can be implemented relatively
easily as an add-on to legislation expected to be considered by this Congress.
With expanded excess land leasing authority, agencies, such as NIST, could use its excess land to invite private sector and academic partners to locate on its campus to enhance public private partnerships that other agencies, such as NASA, have done. Clearer conflict of interest rules from federal researchers could be developed, and new technologies in the federal lab system could be commercialized with new federal tech transfer authority based on best practices from public research universities.

This comment is being submitted on behalf of US Ignite, a nonprofit that convenes stakeholders across the wireless networking and equipment industries to advance wireless networking and “smart community” technologies across the United States, in response to the NIST-2021-0007 Request for Information posted to the Federal Register in November 2021. US Ignite is submitting its comment on the requested "Internet of Things" emerging technology area. Specifically, US Ignite recommends that the federal government should invest $1.5 to $2.5 billion over five years for a Department of Defense (DoD) 5G Rapid Deployment Consortium. The Consortium, in partnership with U.S. companies and organizations, would advance applied research and development (R&D), manufacturing support, and other efforts to develop a U.S. based wireless telecommunications equipment manufacturing ecosystem to support the advancement of 5G in the United States. As a key federal stakeholder in the development of advanced wireless technologies, NIST would have an important role to play in the consortium.
As you likely know, 5G is crucial to the widespread adoption of Internet of Things (IoT) enabled technologies because it provides a faster network that can serve the higher connectivity needs of IoT technologies. The 5G Rapid Deployment Consortium would support the creation of a domestic 5G industry, which would reduce wireless costs for the federal government and the private sector, develop new domestic alternatives for Huawei and other international competitors, and strengthen U.S. national security and global competitiveness. Further details on the current marketplace landscape for 5G and the structure and goals of the 5G Rapid Deployment Consortium are included in the attached white paper. As stated at the start of this paragraph, by helping support the domestic 5G industry, the 5G Rapid Deployment Consortium, acting as a public-private partnership, would help foster the IoT emerging technology area.
In regard to NIST’s request for information on foreign capability and capacity, it is well known that the Chinese government has made substantial investments into 5G, while the U.S. has fallen behind its international competitors in the wireless ecosystem. Telecommunications options at present time either pose national security threats or do not have the capacity to compete globally. In 2020, the Federal Communications Commission designated Chinese telecommunications giants Huawei Technologies Company, the global leader in wireless telecommunications equipment, and ZTE Corporation as national security risks due to connections to the Chinese government and concerns over Chinese national security laws that may require them to support intelligence activities. Other leading companies based in allied nations, such as Nokia and Erickson, do not have the capacity to compete globally and ensure the deployment of next-generation advanced wireless networks will be trusted and secure. The U.S.’ limited domestic options leaves the federal government and US carriers vulnerable to price and production swings and is a critical national security concern. A 5G Rapid Development Consortium would help bring the United States back to the helm of global leadership in advanced telecommunications, guarantee the security of future networks, and ensure standards are set to our values. The United States being a global leader in advanced telecommunications is critical to the secure development and adoption of IoT technologies both within and outside our borders.
Further details on the proposed consortium and its expected impact are provided in the attached white paper. Please do not hesitate to reach out to US Ignite if you are interested in additional information.

Background on US Ignite: US Ignite is a nonprofit that convenes communities, academia, and leaders across the wireless networking and equipment industries to advance wireless networking and “smart community” technologies. US Ignite has eight years of experience managing advanced networking projects that require active participation and contributions by cities and their civic and tech organizations and is the project lead on a number of national programs related to smart cities and advanced wireless development, including the NSF’s Platform for Advanced Wireless Research (PAWR) program and Project OVERCOME. Additional information about US Ignite is available in the attached white paper and at https://www.us-ignite.org/about-what-is-us-ignite/.

comment_text:
Abstract
This paper contends the following: Blockchain as a ledger or immutable database alone is a limited technology with no real use cases. The true value of the technology is apparent through the consensus mechanisms which enable the real value proposition, namely digital value and distributed peer-to-peer trust. This paper outlines why consensus is the true innovation in the blockchain space, some methods of consensus, and applied use cases. Applied use cases discussed: digital tokens; defense applications and distributed trust; IoT and distributed data exchange in industry, including energy. It is important that this reviewing body considers the implications of such a technology in order to create smart policy. Lastly, we encourage regulatory frameworks in the space to focus on enabling technology growth on public, decentralized networks where entrepreneurs can be free to build and innovate.

Introduction
We believe the significance of “Blockchain technology” is the creation of new value models, consensus mechanisms, and tokenization itself, not the “blockchain” technology. Blockchain technology is a broad, oft misused term that people use to describe many things and frequently just an immutable database. An immutable database, while having limited use cases in regulatory and legal cases, is not a revolutionary technology in and of itself. While it’s important to distinguish between much of the current sensational, speculative hype surrounding cryptocurrencies and their derivatives like NFTs, we must also contrast enterprise efforts focused on Blockchain as a limited database technology. Cutting through the confusion, we will look towards the core capabilities of the technology and where this will lead to a future of digital value exchange.

The attached paper further elaborates on the introductory points above.

•Ensure that any future AI standards adequately mitigate risks of bias and promote transparency and explainability; and

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2023-07776
comment_text:
30. What role should government policy have, if any, in the AI accountability ecosystem?

Government policy serves as a critical pillar in the AI accountability ecosystem. It helps establish and enforce norms, enhance transparency, and ensure ethical considerations are factored into AI applications. Much like the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office ensures recognition and binding compensation for inventors, similar structures could be adopted for AI, acknowledging and compensating the collective creators of training data.

To counter the economic displacement caused by AI and to underscore the need for data provenance, policies should include regulations that protect privacy, enforce transparency, prevent harm, and institute accountability and auditing measures. A model worth emulating involves forming regulated bodies that safeguard data producers' interests, control data usage, and ensure income sharing from their data. This will help curb AI's economic disruptions and improve data provenance by necessitating 'watermarking' of transmitted data.

The swift advancements in AI and the significant economic disruptions they cause underscore the need for policy interventions. These policies should recognize and compensate the individuals and communities whose data powers AI technologies, mirroring principles seen in certain legislative efforts.
Data provenance, involving tracking, and documenting data's journey and use, should be a focal point of government policy. This helps facilitate regulatory compliance checks and audits, guaranteeing ethical and lawful AI operations. Furthermore, creating a regulatory body that resolves disputes, enforces privacy and data use standards, and oversees the AI sector, could offer solutions to the complex and evolving issues surrounding AI accountability.

AI accountability policies and/or regulation should be predominantly horizontal, with the foundation of these regulations centered around the management, use, and compensation for data. This horizontal approach cuts across sectors, setting up universal principles and standards for data handling that can apply to every industry where AI is utilized.

While specific use cases of AI can indeed vary across sectors and thus may require nuanced regulation, a horizontal approach ensures a common and fundamental level of accountability, transparency, and fairness in all AI practices, regardless of the industry. This is particularly crucial when we consider that the backbone of all AI systems — the data — is largely agnostic to the end use case.

By focusing on data as the starting point for regulation, governments can ensure that all AI systems, irrespective of their application, adhere to the principles of data provenance, privacy, and fair compensation for the use of individuals' data. This allows for a more streamlined and cohesive oversight, making it easier to audit and hold accountable AI systems in every industry.

Moreover, a horizontal approach to AI accountability helps mitigate the risk of regulatory capture by preventing any particular sector or industry from having undue influence over the rules. This helps create a balanced and fair ecosystem where the interests of all stakeholders, including data providers, AI developers, and end-users, are considered.

(see attachment for answers to additional questions)

Global Partners Digital (GPD) works to ensure that human rights underpin the development, use and governance of digital technologies.

GPD has a long history of engagement within digital policy processes at the global, regional and national levels to ensure that frameworks, norms and standards that govern digital technologies are human rights-respecting. This has included efforts to shape AI laws and policies, particularly through our ongoing engagement at the Council of Europe’s Committee on AI (CAI), which has been tasked with developing the world’s first treaty on AI.

We welcome the opportunity to provide comments on the AI Accountability Policy Request for Comment issued by the National Telecommunications and Information Administration.

GPD is pleased that the government is undertaking this effort to interrogate what effective accountability means in AI policy. AI has been compared in recent days with electricity, as something truly revolutionary that will radically change our lives and power each one of our human activities. Whether this claim becomes true is something that remains to be seen, but what is clear is that AI at its current stage of development is not something that happens against our will, and there is a fundamental opportunity for concerted action by governments, companies, and the general public to ensure that AI is regulated and overseen in a way that mitigates and redresses existing harms and is underpinned by transparency.

In this landscape it is useful to remember that AI is yet another form of technology, hence a human creation. This means that existing frameworks and types of regulations which have been developed in previous decades are still relevant today, and we can use these to guide ongoing efforts to harness the advantages of AI technologies and mitigate its harms. title: Comment on FR Doc # 2023-07776
comment_text:
The AI and the Artist

To all concerned,

There is a lot of noise about generative AI. Tech companies claim it’s a miraculous new gift to humanity, set to push us into new realms of achievement. They are wrong in this. The methodology behind it has been around for millennia. The same technique was used on the woolly mammoth. More recently, it’s been applied to the Western black rhinoceros, the African elephant, and the American buffalo. It’s the same philosophy that justifies strip mining and the cutting of the rainforest: harvest the part you want, then leave the rest to die, rot, and disappear. It has been applied in many ways throughout human history. Now, it is being wielded by generative AI.

I'm a writer. I give up long hours of my time, hustling for words between my 40-hour job, my volunteer work and my dedication to my partner, trying to get further with the novels I'm scratching out. Writing is my main goal in life, and one of the few things that gets me out of bed to keep going. I write maybe 500 words a day on average. When I see people who claim they've "written" 100 books in 9 months (it’s a thing, Google it), it makes me feel like my voice has become obsolete before I've had the chance to say anything. AI companies casually and callously push for more and more power while claiming their product is a tool to help artists, but people like this aren't artists. They're opportunists taking advantage of unregulated technology to make a quick buck by overwhelming a market that's already hard for honest creators to break even in.

People like this claim that AI is the next wave in the Industrial Revolution. That AI is just the powered loom, once again making spinning wheels obsolete. But they dodge the fact that the wool for their power loom is stolen from the spinning wheels they're claiming to improve. No one was sorry to say goodbye to spinning wool. It was drudgery, and automation was a godsend. For artists, the loss of our ability to create and to share our drawings and words and music with the world isn't the loss of some grindy chore we'd happily put aside. It's the loss of a deep and personal part of what makes us human. I can't speak for everyone, but I know that for me, a world where the only thing I'm halfway good at has become a worthless, robotic commodity is a world I have little interest in continuing to walk in.

Some lawmakers are aware of the problems we face in this battle, and we appreciate their support. But there is an issue no one seems to talk about: the cost of copyright. Most of the debates around AI are focused around whether it’s learning from copyrighted material and whether artists are being compensated for their copyrighted work. The problem with this rhetoric is that copyright is expensive. As a novelist, paying $50 to register a book every 2 or 3 years isn’t going to break the bank. For the poems and short stories I write, it becomes a major problem. For visual artists, comic creators, and others who pump out work on a daily basis, constantly registering all their output would be crippling. Training on copyrighted material is a red herring when artists can’t afford to pay for the formal copyright process or to enforce it once granted. Meanwhile, we have obscenely rich tech startups systematically robbing the creative population blind at gigabite speed. Any law or lack of law that allows this theft to continue is not about fair use, it’s about protecting the bully and sending the kid with broken glasses home for fighting.

Thank you for your consideration of this critical issue. Artists don't have many resources to fight companies like this. (We don't get paid much, lol.) I know I’m dramatic—I can’t help it, I’m a novelist. But please take this issue seriously. We look back at the slaughter of the buffalo and the mammoth and shake our heads, calling it a tragic abuse of resources. Yet here we are in the same situation, trying to decide whether to apply that same practice to art. The AI techbois are standing with their spears and rifles ready, hoping for open season on the creative community. If you do nothing, we may be shaking our heads in another hundred years, looking back and wondering why we allowed humanity’s artistic talent to be automated into extinction.

Thank you for listening.
- Christopher Michael Brooke, writer and author

*These words were written by a human, without the use of generative AI

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2023-07776
comment_text:
These comments present the notion of employing liability risk and requiring developers and users of AI applications to obtain insurance (commercial or self-insurance) to indemnify their organization (or as individuals) against litigation and financial losses stemming from substantive harms their system may create.

As shown with cybersecurity issues, when organizations are presented with litigation-driven losses for creating cybersecurity harms, they rely on insurance coverage to protect the organization from financial and organizational harm. That resulted in insurers requiring minimum cybersecurity practices standards of their insured before they would pay out.

This would be coupled with a new set of laws exposing organizations developing, deploying or using AI or related digital applications (to be defined) to risk of significant federal monetary fines (along the lines of the EU's approach of percentages of gross revenues), or in an extreme case, forfeiture of ownership.

Those who deploy or use these systems would be protected from litigation if they engage in demonstrable and credible harm research, tools and mitigation practices to prevent foreseeable harm or act promptly when new harms are discovered.

It is possible that this approach could substitute for government requirements for audits and proofs of system integrity. The challenge with these approaches is that it is likely oversight systems will be unable to keep pace with the evolving technology and creativity of developers. Regrettably, by its nature, government will often be several steps behind.

By requiring non-trivial penalties for failing to prevent harm, organizations will be incentivized to protect themselves financially, and insurers will be motivated to ensure their customers are doing all they can to protect the insurer from liability.

In a way this approach fills the policy gap we have learned from Section 230. The broad protection it granted was not offset with penalties for failing to do so.

At the end of the day, this technology should be subject to the Hippocratic ethos that physicians follow, “first do no harm.”

There is some work to be done to evolve this, but it may be a pathway. The attached paper goes into more detail.

comment_text:
On behalf of the Center for AI and Digital Policy (CAIDP) we attach our statement in response to the Request for Comments (RFC) issued by the NTIA on Artificial Intelligence (“AI”) system accountability measures and policies. In our Comments we (1) provide General Recommendations on AI Accountability and (2) provide specific responses to Questions 1, 4, 5, 9, 16, 20, 25, 26, and 34.

In summary, we recommend:

1.Companies should not release AI products that are not safe. President Biden has said directly, at least twice, that tech companies have a responsibility to make sure their products are safe before making them public.

2.Human-centric accountability practices must protect fundamental rights, democratic values, and the rule of law.

3.Accountability mechanisms must incorporate best practices set out in the Universal Guidelines for Artificial Intelligence , the OECD AI Principles and the UNESCO Recommendation on AI Ethics .

4.Accountability should be based on mandatory impact assessments, audits, and certifications throughout the AI lifecycle to ensure transparency, auditability, contestability, and traceability.

5.Legal standards should be established to ensure AI accountability. Accountability mechanisms or practices will have no meaningful impact in the absence of clearly defined legal standards and enforceable remedies.

6.The United States should support a comprehensive international treaty for AI to ensure accountability across the public and private sectors.

comment_text:
The request for comment included:

3. AI accountability measures have been proposed in connection with many different goals, including … [t]here has been adequate transparency and explanation to affected people about the uses, capabilities, and limitations of the AI system.

5. Given the likely integration of generative AI tools such as large language models (e.g., ChatGPT) or other general-purpose AI or foundational models into downstream products, how can AI accountability mechanisms inform people about how such tools are operating and/or whether the tools comply with standards for trustworthy AI?

11. What lessons can be learned from accountability processes and policies in cybersecurity, privacy, finance, or other areas? 

23. How should AI accountability “products” (e.g., audit results) be communicated to different stakeholders? Should there be standardized reporting within a sector and/or across sectors?

Similarly, at a hearing on May 16, 2023, Senator Richard Blumenthal asked OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, “[s]hould we consider independent testing labs to provide scorecards and nutrition labels, or the equivalent of nutrition labels, packaging, that indicates to people whether or not the content can be trusted, what the ingredients are?”

I submit this comment in response to those questions. For seventeen years, I have represented injured consumers, employees, and patients in personal injury, product liability, and workplace safety claims. My work routinely involves corporations that have failed to warn about a risk or to follow a regulatory safety standard. I have litigated claims involving CPSC-recalled consumer products, EPA regulation of hazardous chemicals, EPA labeling of pesticides, FDA approval of medical devices, FDA approval of pharmaceutical labeling, USCG-enforced inland navigation rules, OSHA requirements for personal protective equipment, and NHTSA crash test standards.

If generative AI is as powerful and transformative as its proponents say, then it should be held to at least the same standards of honesty and transparency as a pack of gum. Currently, the AI companies deny they have any responsibility to consumers at all.

For further details, see the full attached comment, in which I discuss model cards and the current state of AI model disclosure, the underlying problem of AI terms of service disclaiming all representations and waiving all liability, examples of other product disclosures (nutrition labels, safety data sheets, and prescribing information), and note the parallels between the Gebru / Bender / Mitchell framework and pharmaceutical labeling, and recommend similar disclosures to protect consumers.

Requiring standardized labeling would of course not resolve every policy issue raised by generative AI, but it would help lessen accidental misuse of the technology. It would also help impose discipline on an industry prone to overstating the technology’s current capabilities while simultaneously disclaiming all representations and warranties in the fine print.

comment_text:
In my response, I'll be referring the the questions provided in the request for comment by question number and subsection.
The text of these questions is not included for brevity's sake, but added a pdf version with the written questions included.

Existing Resources and Models

9.
Currently, most foundational AI systems developed are free and open source- that means that source code and models are made available to the public and permission is granted to them to examine, modify, use, and redistribute the models and code. Since the code and models are freely available, they are are constantly being examined by companies, scientists, and everyday programmers who seek to improve the project and verify safety and security. The open source model of self regulation operates very well as an accountability measure for honest development and works wonderfully to prevent any malicious actors who would seek to undermine security, privacy, or safety. The Federal government currently recognizes the benefits of the transparency, cost, maintenance, and re-usability of open source code compared to proprietary code (see 'Federal Source Code Policy.pdf' attached)

Accountability Subjects

15a.
A company using the AI system should be held liable for discriminatory behavior if they use an AI system that discriminates based on protected characteristics, with a sliding scale of severity based on the amount of checks and balances present or absent in the company to prevent such discrimination. If the company used a third party AI system intended for their field without modification, that system should be audited, with the third party assuming liability on the basis of the outcome.

15c.
Just a few days ago in State of New Jersey v. Francisco Arteaga, the court held that defendant Francisco Arteaga must be provided with the facial recognition technology and data used to identify him (see 'New Jersey v. Francisco Arteaga.pdf' attached). Just like in this case, the best way to identify potential illegal discrimination in sensitive fields and reassure the public is to provide individuals with access to their data which the AI system used, and proactively providing access of the technology and source code to perform an individual examination. If the individual identifies an issue they believe resulted in illegal discrimination, they can submit a request for a formal audit. This ensures a robust accountability system that has AI systems either follow any new anti-discrimination regulation, or quickly fail under scrutiny. A company shouldn’t require customers to waive liability for illegal discrimination in exchange for their this information or service.

15d.
Upstream implementations can’t reasonably predict all the ultimate downstream implementations, and shouldn’t be held accountable for any misuse by bad actors. Upstream implementations should only be held accountable for instances where they are very close to the downstream implementation, like if they were directly commissioned to create the AI system, or they provided closed access to those they knew definitively had intent to misuse and abuse the AI system.

AI Accountability Policies

30a.
AI accountability should depend on business sector. Chat-bots, image generators, text-to-speech audio, and other AI can be used to serve a creative purpose. Due to it’s potential for artistic use and in order to preserve the integrity of the 1st Amendment, I am speaking in opposition to any required certification, testing, licensing, fees, harmful bias mitigation, discrimination protections, or audits for AI models with creative applications. America doesn’t require citizens to pass a test and pay a fee to obtain a speech license and doesn’t limit what they say to only approved speech- and I’m certain the implementation of such a system for Generative AI would abridge the freedom of speech. However, there is a difference between using an image generator to draw a picture, and using it in a police investigation. Liability is a concern for non-creative applications in areas like education, law, and finance. While each of these fields could benefit from AI services, a blanket AI accountability regulation would be ill suited for each of them. It would be best to tailor fit AI accountability to each sector.

title: Comment on OMB-2023-0020-0001
comment_text:
First, we caution against overloading civil servants with additional steps they have to take to ensure responsible AI. Any such activities should not be additive to already existing sets of expertise and workloads, but compliment them. This can best be done by identifying units and individuals who already are entrusted with responsible-AI related concerns (such as research and development, procurement, or compliance). The new responsible AI mandates outlined in the OMB implementation guidelines should be mapped onto the work that these units already do. In previous work, we have called this approach “Practice-Based Compliance Framework”.

Second, we urge agencies to consider their own employees as key stakeholders in the responsible AI space. Responsible AI-focused stakeholder engagement efforts, such as sandboxes, discussion groups, or surveys, such decidedly include this stakeholder group. We underline that this type of stakeholder engagement can not be conducted in a one-size-fits-all fashion. Rather, it should fold into organization- and agency-specific environments. Internal stakeholder engagement in one agency will look different from stakeholder engagement in another agency. We have discussed what that can look like in the context of AI procurement, explaining how agencies and units can avoid common traps.

Third, it is crucial that compliance with the OMB implementation guidelines should not rely solely on data, measurements, and risk accounting provided by AI vendors. Assessing impacts on the terms set by those being assessed risks does not produce robust accountability to the public interest. When vendors define risks and impacts in ways that ensure a favorable assessment for their products, they are only accountable to themselves. This is avoidable by ensuring independent evaluators are permitted to conduct their own real-world tests and produce their own documentation of AI systems, where appropriate.

Pertaining to 5.b.ii., we want to underline that AI systems that purport to be “detecting or measuring emotions, thought, or deception in humans” are often based on pseudo-scientific constructs and plagued by instability, leading to invalidity of these tools as test instruments. Additionally, constructs that are scientific are not necessarily observable (such as socioeconomic status, teacher effectiveness, and risk of recidivism) and must be inferred from measurements of observable properties. This process necessarily involves making assumptions, introducing the potential for mismatches between the understanding of the construct purported to be measured and how it is operationalized in an AI system. Many AI harms are direct results of such mismatches. An AI assessment should, therefore, include a careful check of the assumptions and constructs that underpin an AI system. Such assessments can and should be incorporated into procurement processes.

Relatedly, we want to comment on 5.c.iv. and underline that AI impact assessments should always include qualitative analysis (such as of the scientific history and validity of a construct, and its underpinning assumptions). Qualitative and quantitative assessments must be meaningfully integrated. How this can be done has, for example, been proposed in the “Love Triangle” framework that combines assumptions tracking with statistical stability analysis into a holistic AI audit approach. This approach has already been put into practice.

Hardware- and sensor-driven systems (such as motion capture technology) should not be exempt from AI assessments. Hardware components carry their own, potentially harmful, assumptions and design features. One historical example of this is the way color photographic film was calibrated to render lighter skin tones more accurately than darker skin tones, which was then propagated into color calibration for digital photographic technologies. These hardware-related considerations should be assessed as part of an AI assessment, not least to avoid harms and risk an approach that is overtly data-centric.

It is important that good documentation and archiving practices be developed for these types of holistic AI assessments, and that respective archives be publicly accessible and carefully maintained. This should be considered public interest technology infrastructure and be federally funded.

Lastly, we recommend carefully considering the framing and execution of “consult and incorporate feedback from affected groups” (5.c.v.B). It is important to approach engagement with affected groups from a non-extractive standpoint, not least to avoid superficial “participation-washing”. Affected groups must be carefully and consensually enrolled in feedback processes and they must be compensated for their time and expertise. At the same time, these kinds of infrastructures for soliciting this type of feedback must be aligned with the principles of equity and dignity, and they must be sustainably funded.

In accordance with the Biden Administration’s Executive Order on the Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence, “OMB has prepared a draft memorandum that would direct Federal agencies to strengthen their AI governance and innovation programs while managing risks from the use of AI, particularly when that use affects the safety and rights of the public.”

As you may know, PSC is an industry association with more than 400 member companies—small, mid-sized, and large—that provide much-needed technology and professional services to all federal agencies. These companies and their workers throughout America and around the world are equally as committed to U.S. Government missions as federal civilian and uniformed personnel. PSC supports our members and their federal government customers by promoting effective government practices and policies, improvements in federal contracting, and constructive dialogue between government and industry. We anticipate that government policy decisions around AI’s application in the broader commercial environment—and how those decisions will impact government missions—will affect the federal contracting community.

With that in mind, the federal government must get its approach to AI policy on a good path from the outset: that policy will impact both the federal programs that create requirements, issue contracts and task orders, and assess performance on desired outcomes and those companies that offer and deliver solutions to their federal customers. OMB’s eight questions within the request for comments reflect a good starting point for a broad dialogue regarding the effective development, use, and management of rapidly evolving AI technologies. We look forward to additional opportunities to provide industry perspectives as the government refines its policies and guidance regarding AI use cases. PSC respectfully offers to help facilitate substantive engagements between your office and industry as appropriate and to help deepen understanding between public and private sector officials regarding the possibilities and potential limits of AI use going forward.

Specifically with regard to those eight OMB questions within the Federal Register notice, PSC offers a range of comments below that reflect PSC member company feedback. We acknowledge that perspectives in this fast-changing area of AI technologies may evolve as we learn more about AI tools and explore their uses, and we again note that OMB’s questions represent a solid starting point to these discussions.

Please see attached letter for these specific comments.

comment_text:
Broaden the Scope of AI Impact Considerations: While the document focuses on the safety and rights of the public impacted by AI, it could benefit from explicitly including considerations for groups typically underrepresented in technology development and governance. This would involve assessing the impact of AI on diverse communities, including those discriminated against due to work and descent​​.

Inclusive Language in AI Governance: When discussing AI governance, ensure that the language used reflects a commitment to diversity and inclusion. This could include emphasizing the role of the Chief AI Officer (CAIO) in promoting inclusive AI practices and ensuring that AI governance structures are representative of diverse perspectives​​.

Emphasizing Equity in AI Innovation: While discussing responsible AI innovation, explicitly include the goal of advancing equity. This would involve ensuring that AI development and adoption do not exacerbate existing inequalities but rather contribute to reducing them, especially for marginalized and underserved communities​​.

Risk Management with an Equity Lens: In managing risks from the use of AI, explicitly incorporate an equity lens. This means not only considering the direct risks to safety and rights but also how AI applications might perpetuate systemic biases or inequalities. This approach ensures that risk management practices are sensitive to the needs and contexts of diverse populations​​.

Comprehensive Compliance with Inclusion Policies: Ensure that AI-related policies and practices are in alignment with broader federal policies on equity, diversity, and inclusion. This alignment helps in creating a holistic approach to AI governance and innovation that is inclusive and representative of all community needs​​.

Stakeholder Engagement: Encourage agencies to engage with a wide range of stakeholders, including those from underserved and marginalized communities, in the development, deployment, and governance of AI. title: Comment from Stephen Lawton
comment_text:
Please see the enclosed PDF with 8 questions answered. I concluded my answers with the following:

I support the overall goals of the draft memorandum, which are to advance responsible AI innovation and to manage the risks associated with the use of AI by federal agencies. I believe that the memorandum provides a good framework for agencies to develop and implement effective AI governance programs.

With that being said, my key concern is who Nvidia is allowed to do business with.

Here are some factors to consider when making this decision:
•The entity's track record of responsible AI use.
•The entity's commitment to human rights and ethical values.
•The potential for the entity to use NVIDIA products for malicious purposes.
•The benefits of allowing the entity to use NVIDIA products, such as the advancement of scientific research or the development of new products and services.
It is also important to note that NVIDIA has a number of policies and procedures in place to mitigate the risks of its products being used for malicious purposes. For example, NVIDIA has a Code of Conduct that prohibits its employees and customers from using NVIDIA products for illegal or unethical purposes. NVIDIA also has a number of technical safeguards in place to prevent its products from being used for malicious purposes, such as encryption and authentication.
Ultimately, the decision of whether or not to allow NVIDIA to do business with a particular entity is a complex one that must be made on a case-by-case basis. There is no easy answer, and there will always be some risk involved. However, by carefully considering the factors discussed above, decision-makers can help to ensure that NVIDIA products are used for good and not for harm.
In the specific case of Del Complex, I would recommend that OMB carefully consider the company's plan to develop AI offshore with lax regulations or no regulations at all. This raises concerns about the company's commitment to responsible AI use and human rights. Additionally, Del Complex's plan to launch barges into international waters beginning next year to develop AI outside of the reach of regulators is concerning. This plan could make it more difficult to oversee and mitigate the risks associated with Del Complex's use of AI.
Overall, I believe that the risks of allowing NVIDIA to do business with Del Complex outweigh the benefits. I urge OMB to disallow NVIDIA from providing H100 GPUs to Del Complex.

title: Comment on OMB-2023-0020-0001
comment_text:
The City of San José Information Technology Department appreciates the opportunity to submit comments in response to the request for comment on the proposed draft memorandum titled “Advancing Governance, Innovation, and Risk Management for Agency Use of Artificial Intelligence” by the Office of Management and Budget (the OMB Memo).

In late 2022, the Digital Privacy Office (DPO) began the initial governance of AI systems as a natural extension of governing data policies and data processing. Starting with procurement reviews, the City’s AI governance has evolved into Generative AI initiatives, and impact assessments. Recently, San José began a coalition of over 100 state and local agencies to build a standardized approach to AI governance, policy, and vendor accountability. We hope to connect the Coalition’s work with the efforts at OMB and the broader Federal government.
Summary of Comments
We celebrate the OMB memo as a vital step towards comprehensive AI policy for U.S. public agencies.

•Chief AI Officer (CAIO): Our experience at San José has demonstrated the need for a designated lead on AI policy and governance. The CAIO needs to lead across AI governance, procurement, and technical projects. This ensures all AI projects follow responsible AI governance and fosters mutual maturity between policy and practical implementation of technology. The City’s CAIO function is currently served by technical and project management leads with the Digital Privacy Officer, but may vary based on where technology policies are managed in an agency.

•Leveraging existing governing bodies: The City has leveraged its Digital Privacy Officer and existing privacy and data governing bodies to handle AI governance. The City found that stakeholders for both Privacy and AI overlapped considerably, and we recommend exploring if the same is true at your agencies to minimize additional overhead.

•Vendor accountability: When implementing our impact assessment framework at the City of San José, we experienced varying levels of cooperation across vendors in obtaining information around the “nutrition facts” of their AI systems. Larger vendors were often unresponsive or unwilling to provide us information about the AI system. Having a standardized “nutrition facts” requirement for all AI systems enforced at the federal level would solve this problem.

•Generative AI: Agencies should leverage generative AI tools for creating initial drafts of content while establishing safeguards to ensure responsible use. To promote the responsible use of generative AI tools, the City of San José and many others have released Generative AI Guidelines to help City employees leverage the benefits of generative AI tools while understanding and mitigating its risks.

•Minimum practices: The minimum practices outlined in the memo may be too aggressive for agencies to implement by the desired timeline. Agencies with a lower AI maturity may struggle to successfully implement all minimum requirements by the deadline.

Our detailed comments can be found in the attached document titled "231205 OMB Public Comment City of San José". Additional attachments are explained in our detailed comments.

title: Comment on OMB-2023-0020-0001
comment_text:
Attached are comments from CAP, Public Citizen, Public Knowledge, and numerous other organizations in response to the Request for Comments: Advancing Governance, Innovation, and Risk Management for Agency Use of Artificial Intelligence Draft Memorandum.

Throughout 2023, numerous civil, technology, and human rights groups called for the Executive Branch to take immediate executive action on artificial intelligence (AI)i and to center the White House Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights. The President’s Executive Order on the Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI EO) represents a strong start on the guidance needed to ensure the development of safe and effective AI.iv The accompanying draft OMB guidance, “Advancing Governance, Innovation, and Risk Management for Agency Use of Artificial Intelligence,” represents essential and needed guidance for federal agencies, contractors, and grantees that are already using AI systems.

We believe it is essential to meaningfully center civil rights and equity in the implementation of these executive actions. Most centrally, that means building on the AI Bill of Rights and requiring that AI systems be shown to be effective, safe, and nondiscriminatory before use; further enumerating rights-impacting and safety-impacting uses that inherently pose the greatest risk; ensuring a broad scope by strengthening procurement language and increasing specificity around waivers and exemptions; ensuring adequate resourcing for implementation; and publishing guidance prior to using generative AI. Agencies should also consider alternative solutions when evaluating AI systems and continue to inventory their AI regulatory authority. Attached, we provide brief comments on each of these elements.

title: Comment from Fred Oswald
comment_text:
This brief comment is to emphasize worker, workforce, and organization-relevant implications of the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) draft memorandum, "Advancing Governance, Innovation, and Risk Management for Agency Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)." In particular, AI and machine learning in all their various forms:

* will likely accelerate in their abilities (a) to create opportunities for new jobs and entire occupations, (b) to alter required job skills for existing jobs fundamentally, and (c) to replace certain jobs or essential job tasks (Selenko et al., 2022);

* require a continuous re-examination of the knowledge, skills, abilities, and other essential worker requirements across occupations (National Center for O*NET Development, 2023), with wide-ranging implications for both workers and the workforce;

* carry major implications for both technical and socio-technical aspects of AI-specific education and workforce training (NAIAC, 2023), as well as the reskilling of existing worker skills that have been fundamentally altered by AI tools and systems;

* alter the nature of organizational systems of recruiting, hiring, training, and promoting, and the manner in which these functions will be conducted.

OMB guidance will stand to benefit from considering all these interrelated points above and how they can lead to tangible actions for assessing, forecasting, intervening, and improving the AI workforce across federal agencies. The end goal is to improve AI infrastructure within federal agencies and in their relationships with one another. This not only means increasing workers' AI-related capabilities and capacities in terms of their own functioning; it also means equipping workers with the ability to assess the nature and balance of AI benefits and risks adequately, taking into account the broader sociotechnical work environment in which AI and machine learning systems operate.

In closing, please note that I am a member of the National Artificial Intelligence Advisory Committee (NAIAC), but I speak here in my own personal capacity.

Best regards,
Fred Oswald
Professor and Herbert S. Autrey Chair in Social Sciences
Rice University

comment_text:
Re: Request for Comments: Advancing Governance, Innovation, and Risk Management for Agency Use of Artificial Intelligence Draft Memorandum; FR Doc. 2023-24269, 23 Nov. 2023.

Dear Ms. Martorana,

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has the potential to dramatically impact nearly all the federal government’s operations and engagement with the American people. The opportunities and risks of AI, combined with the power of the state, places an even greater burden on the federal government to ensure its ethical use of AI, especially when AI is used for purposes that impact safety or rights. The federal government, its contractors, and its grantees’ use of AI should only be allowed if those AI systems are effective, safe, and nondiscriminatory.

The Center for American Progress (CAP) has called for the Executive Branch to take immediate action on AI and has joined the civil rights community and other allies in advocating for centering the White House Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights (AI Bill of Rights) in any AI executive order (EO) and Office of Management and Budget (OMB) guidance. The President’s Executive Order on the Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI EO) represents a strong start on the guidance needed to ensure the development of safe and effective AI.

The accompanying draft OMB guidance “Advancing Governance, Innovation, and Risk Management for Agency Use of Artificial Intelligence” is essential guidance for federal agencies and contractors that are already using AI systems. Particularly worthy of praise is the draft guidance’s definition of safety-impacting and rights-impacting AI and purposes that are presumed to be safety-impacting and rights-impacting. These thoughtful definitions are an important step forward in outlining the conditions in which the use of AI requires extra attention and caution.

Sincerely,
